common_name: Serena Angelonia (Compact Seed-Grown Heat-Tolerant Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Transplant after the last frost into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Serena is seed-grown rather than a cutting-propagated series, giving growers an economical way to fill beds with heat-proof color through the worst of Gulf South summer.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing plants 8–12 inches apart for a dense, mounded bed. Serena was one of the first widely available seed-propagated angelonia series, developed to bring the heat and humidity tolerance of vegetatively propagated angelonia to growers at a lower cost, and it forms compact, well-branched mounds covered in snapdragon-like spikes in purple, pink, blue, and white from late spring through frost. It needs no deadheading to rebloom and holds up remarkably well through the peak heat and rain of a Gulf Coast summer when many other bedding annuals decline. Light, regular feeding and even moisture keep the mounded habit dense and floriferous; established plantings tolerate short dry spells without collapsing.
sources: PanAmerican Seed — Serena angelonia series notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bedding Plant Trials

common_name: Miss Kim Lilac (Compact Late-Blooming Fragrant Korean Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; Miss Kim blooms about two weeks later than common lilac, which helps its flowers dodge a late frost, and it tolerates more heat and humidity than most lilac cultivars.

directions: Plant in full sun with good air circulation in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and prune spent flower clusters right after bloom since next year's buds set soon after. Miss Kim is a compact selection of Manchurian lilac introduced from the US National Arboretum, prized for dense, rounded growth that stays smaller than common lilac, intensely fragrant lavender-purple flower clusters that open later and last longer, and foliage that turns burgundy-purple in fall. Its better tolerance of heat and humidity than Syringa vulgaris makes it one of the more dependable lilacs for the warmer edge of lilac-growing range, though it still wants a real winter chill to bloom well and struggles in the Deep South's mildest zones. Established shrubs are long-lived and low-maintenance, needing only post-bloom deadheading and an occasional renewal cane removed at the base to stay vigorous.

common_name: Palibin Dwarf Korean Lilac (Compact Long-Lived Fragrant Dwarf Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; Palibin's naturally dwarf, dense habit needs no shearing to keep a tidy rounded form, making it useful for foundation plantings and low hedges.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and prune only lightly right after bloom to remove spent flower heads, since Palibin naturally keeps a dense, rounded, proportionate form without regular shearing. This dwarf Korean lilac is smothered each spring in masses of small, intensely fragrant pale lavender-pink flower panicles that are proportionate to its compact size, unlike many lilacs where large blooms overwhelm a small shrub. Its naturally tidy habit, fine-textured blue-green foliage, and good resistance to powdery mildew have made it one of the most widely planted dwarf lilacs for foundation plantings, mixed borders, and low informal hedges. Like other lilacs it needs real winter chill to flower reliably and performs best at the cooler end of its hardiness range, but established plants are tough, long-lived, and essentially maintenance-free.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Bloomerang Lilac (Reblooming Dwarf Lilac with Spring and Summer Flushes)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; deadhead the heavy spring flush promptly to encourage the intermittent summer and fall rebloom this series is bred for.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and deadhead spent spring flower clusters promptly to redirect energy into the intermittent summer rebloom this series was bred to produce. Bloomerang, developed by Proven Winners, was among the first lilacs marketed specifically for reblooming, opening a full flush of fragrant purple-lavender flowers in spring like a standard lilac and then continuing to produce scattered new blooms on current-season wood through summer and into fall. Its compact, rounded habit fits smaller gardens and foundation plantings better than large old-fashioned lilac shrubs, and it shares the family's need for a real winter chill and good air circulation to perform and stay free of powdery mildew. Light monthly feeding and consistent moisture through summer support the extended rebloom cycle better than the sparser feeding a once-blooming lilac needs.
sources: Proven Winners — Bloomerang lilac series notes

common_name: Fine Wine Weigela (Compact Dark-Purple-Foliage Weigela with Rose-Pink Flowers)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; foliage color and bloom are both best with at least six hours of direct sun, though the shrub tolerates part shade.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and prune lightly right after the main spring flush to shape the compact mound without removing next year's buds. Fine Wine is a dwarf sport of the popular dark-leaved Wine and Roses weigela, bred smaller still for tight spaces, foundation plantings, and mixed containers, with narrow, deep burgundy-purple foliage that holds its color through the growing season and clusters of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers in late spring that draw hummingbirds. Its compact, mounded habit needs little pruning to stay tidy, and the dark foliage provides season-long color contrast in a border even between bloom flushes. Established plants are drought-tolerant and largely trouble-free, needing only an occasional renewal cut to the oldest wood to keep growth vigorous.
sources: Proven Winners — Fine Wine weigela notes
